naples.intro: Naples has more catalogued monumental trees than any other Italian city, and keeps the best of them in two places worth a morning each. The Real Bosco di Capodimonte is a former Bourbon hunting estate the court spent two centuries filling with specimens from China, Mexico and Australia, and twelve of these trees grow there. The second walk is the Real Orto Botanico, founded by decree in 1807, where seven more stand within 150 metres, including the widest trunk on the city's register. The rest are scattered across the city.
naples.meta_description: Naples's most remarkable trees, in two walks: the Bourbon estate at Capodimonte with its 220-year-old camphor, and the 1807 botanical garden on Via Foria.
naples.question_answer: Naples's oldest documented tree is the Canforo del Giardino dei Principi, a camphor tree in the Real Bosco di Capodimonte planted in the early 1800s and roughly 220 years old, brought directly from China during the Bourbon era. It grows in the Garden of the Princes, a free section of the park in the north of the city.
naples.question_meta: Naples's oldest tree is a 220-year-old camphor at Capodimonte, brought from China by the Bourbons. Its story, and thirty more trees.
naples.question_context: Naples tops Italy's own official register of monumental trees, the national list created under a 2013 law, with more catalogued specimens than any other municipality in the country. Most of that count concentrates in one place, the Real Bosco di Capodimonte, the former Bourbon royal hunting estate whose Garden of the Princes and Royal Orchard the park's own museum has singled out as home to six specifically monumental trees. Among those, the camphor tree of the Garden of the Princes is the one most consistently dated, at roughly 220 years old, brought from China in the early 1800s and now one of the largest camphor trees anywhere in Europe. A second camphor in the nearby Royal Orchard and a Montezuma cypress share the same garden but only carry a broad 19th century estimate, undated precisely by any single source, a gap common to several other trees on this list. Even the registers disagree at times: for a plane by the Capodimonte pheasantry, the national list gives a trunk 4.3 metres round and the regional one 1.7. The park is free to enter in most sections.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Naples?
faq.a: The Canforo del Giardino dei Principi, a camphor tree in the Real Bosco di Capodimonte, planted in the early 1800s and roughly 220 years old. It grows in the free Garden of the Princes section of the park.

faq.q: Why does Capodimonte have so many of Naples's oldest trees?
faq.a: Because the Bourbon kings spent roughly two centuries turning a royal hunting estate into a working botanical showcase, importing camphor from China, cypress from Mexico and eucalyptus from Australia. Twelve of the thirty-one trees on this list, and more than half of Naples's officially catalogued monumental trees citywide, grow within its 134 hectares.

faq.q: What happened to the famous Pino di Posillipo?
faq.a: The original stone pine, planted after 1855 and one of the most photographed trees in the world through Naples's postcard era, was felled in 1984 after disease. The environmental group Legambiente replanted a new pine on the same spot in 1995, which the group still marks the anniversary of every year. The tree visible today is that younger replacement, not the original.

faq.q: Are Naples's remarkable trees free to see?
faq.a: Almost all of them, in free public parks, squares, a cemetery and a state archive courtyard. The exception is the park of the Mostra d'Oltremare, home to a Moreton Bay fig and a tipu tree, which opens from 7:00 to sunset with a small day ticket and can close for trade fairs. Elsewhere hours matter more than price. The Real Orto Botanico is free but opens on weekdays only, until 14:00 on Monday, Wednesday and Friday and 16:00 on Tuesday and Thursday, so its seven trees cannot be seen at a weekend.

caserta.intro: Caserta's remarkable trees spread well beyond the palace. Sixteen stand inside the English Garden of the Reggia, 23 hectares Maria Carolina had planted in 1786 as Italy's first landscape garden, past a cedar seven and three quarter metres round, a Douglas fir of forty metres and a plane that grew sideways. A bunya pine grows near the palace end of the Royal Park and a magnolia free at the palace gate. Three more stand free in Piazza Vanvitelli, two giants share the town cemetery, and a plane almost five metres round anchors the silk village of San Leucio.
caserta.meta_description: Caserta's monumental trees: sixteen in the Reggia's English Garden, a cedar 7.75 m round among them, and free giants in town and at San Leucio.
caserta.question_meta: Caserta's oldest tree is almost certainly the yew at the Bath of Venus, already mature when it was set in place in the 1790s.
caserta.question_answer: Caserta's oldest tree is almost certainly the European yew at the Bath of Venus, in the English Garden of the Reggia. The Campania regional register calls it one of the patriarchs of the garden and records that it was already a mature tree when it was put in place at the garden's creation in the 1790s, which puts it comfortably past 250 years even though the age field on the same record says only 150. The Douglas fir and the camphor tree a few hundred metres downhill are each given about 200 years, and no tree in Caserta has been dated by counting rings.
caserta.question_context: Every age on this page comes from one place, the Campania regional register of monumental trees, and every age on it is an eta presunta, an estimate. The national MASAF register lists the same trees with the same girths and heights but carries no age field at all, and for the trees outside the Reggia, in the cemetery, San Leucio and the Royal Park, it is the only record, so those carry no age. That matters more here than in most cities, because almost nothing in the English Garden is native and almost nothing was planted before 1786. Maria Carolina commissioned the garden that year on the advice of Sir William Hamilton, the British ambassador in Naples, and John Andrew Graefer, the gardener sent to build it, spent a decade collecting exotics from Capri, Salento and Palermo. So most of these trees are between 150 and 240 years old, and where a register says 200 it means the first planting rather than a measurement. The park also loses trees in storms, most recently a monumental Monterey cypress in December 2019, so treat any single specimen as something to check before a long trip.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Caserta?
faq.a: The yew at the Bath of Venus, in the English Garden of the Reggia. The regional register says it was already a mature tree when it was set there in the 1790s, so it predates the garden. The Douglas fir and the camphor are each given about 200 years.

faq.q: Do you have to pay to see them?
faq.a: For the seventeen inside the Reggia, yes. Sixteen stand in the English Garden, covered by the combined Royal Park and English Garden ticket, 9 euro plus a 1 euro online fee (a 3 euro park-only ticket exists but excludes the English Garden; closed Tuesdays), and a bunya pine grows near the palace end of the Royal Park. Seven are free: a magnolia at the palace gate on Piazza Carlo di Borbone, a monkey puzzle, a casuarina and a yew in Piazza Vanvitelli, a cedar and a camphor in the municipal cemetery, and a plane in Piazza della Seta, San Leucio.

In parts. Inside the English Garden, most of the garden trees stand in the same stretch of the flat southern Palco and the paths just above it, with the yew and one Osage orange further up; getting there is roughly 2.5 km from the palace gate along the main axis, or take the electric shuttle. The bunya pine and the magnolia are near the palace end. The three trees in Piazza Vanvitelli stand within fifty metres of each other in the town centre, the cemetery pair about fifteen metres apart on the east side of town, and the San Leucio plane about 3.5 km north-west of the station.

The sweet osmanthus. The national register credits it with 6.5 metres of trunk; the regional one explains that this is every stem added together, because the species grows as a bundle. In autumn it produces a scent of apricot from flowers a few millimetres wide.

benevento.intro: Benevento's two registered giants share one city park, the Villa Comunale, about ten minutes' walk from the town centre. On the park's belvedere terrace a holm oak four and a half metres round spreads its limbs over the benches, the native evergreen oak of southern Italy at full width. About a hundred metres away a coast redwood from California rises to 33 metres, fifteen metres taller. Both are free to see in an open city park, and together they make a short walk.
benevento.meta_description: Benevento's monumental trees: a holm oak 4.55 m round on the Villa Comunale terrace and a coast redwood 33 m tall, a hundred metres apart.
benevento.question_meta: Benevento's most remarkable tree is a holm oak 4.55 metres round, spreading over the belvedere terrace of the Villa Comunale.
benevento.question_answer: Benevento's most remarkable tree is the holm oak of the Villa Comunale, 4.55 metres round and 18 metres tall on Italy's national register of monumental trees. It spreads in several great limbs over the benches of the park's belvedere terrace. Nobody has published its age, so which tree in the city is oldest remains an open question.
benevento.question_context: Both of Benevento's trees here come from Italy's national register of monumental trees, which records girth and height but no age, and neither has a published planting record. So the city's oldest tree cannot honestly be named. What can be said is which is biggest. The holm oak on the belvedere terrace of the Villa Comunale has the thickest trunk, 455 centimetres, and the register records no other holm oak that size in the park. A naturalist photographed it in July 2024, a wide, many-limbed tree with benches in its shade and a viewpoint rail beside it. The coast redwood, about a hundred metres away, wins on height at 33 metres against the oak's 18, and naturalists recorded redwoods in the park in 2021 and 2024. The two make a natural pair, a native evergreen oak that spreads sideways and an imported conifer that only goes up. The park is free and open air, about ten minutes on foot from the centre and about 1.5 km from the station. If you know when either tree was planted, tell us.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Benevento?
faq.a: Nobody has published a date for any of them. The biggest is the holm oak on the belvedere terrace of the Villa Comunale, 4.55 metres round, and if you know when it was planted, tell us.

Both stand in the Villa Comunale, the city park on Piazza IV Novembre, about ten minutes' walk from the town centre and about 1.5 km from the station. The holm oak is on the belvedere terrace and the redwood about a hundred metres away.

faq.q: Do you have to pay to see them?
faq.a: No. The Villa Comunale is a free, open-air city park.
